Aeolsklavier（風琴鋼琴）是 aeolodion的改良型鍵盤氣鳴樂器，: The Aeolsklavier is an improved keyboard aerophone of the aeolodion type, made about 1825. It uses extremely thin slips of wood rather than metal reeds or springs to sound, and its timbre is softer and sweeter. The player chooses the pitch on the keyboard and works a pedal that drives a separate bellows for each note, producing a soft, drifting sound. The source names no particular player or occasion; all that is known is that the instrument did not catch on and seems to have been quickly forgotten.
來源未載明風琴鋼琴實際出現的音樂場合、類型或編制。它僅被描述為未成功，似乎很快被: The source does not state which musical occasions, genres or ensembles the Aeolsklavier actually appeared in. It is described only as unsuccessful and apparently quickly forgotten, so there are no definite works or performance records to serve as listening examples. Related instruments of the same family have records of accompanying plainchant in small chapels or of appearing at Chopin recitals, but the source does not attribute those occasions to the Aeolsklavier itself.
演奏 Aeolsklavier 時，操作順序為以腳踩踏板，驅動與各音相連的風箱，: To play the Aeolsklavier you step on the pedal, which drives the bellows connected to each note, and then press a key, which sets the thin wooden reed sounding. For a beginner the difficulty is coordinating pedal and keyboard: the bellows must start together with the key press for the sound to come out soft and airy. Because every note has its own bellows, the learner has to become familiar with the pedal and key action at each position and work gradually towards a continuous performance.
約一八〇〇年，漢堡的Jean Tobié Eschenbach製出aeolodi: About 1800 Jean Tobié Eschenbach of Hamburg built the aeolodion; about 1825 Karl Friedrich Emanuel Schortmann of Buttelstedt replaced the metal reeds with thin wooden ones and added a keyboard and pedal-driven bellows, producing the Aeolsklavier. Afterwards instruments of this kind were largely replaced by the reed organ.

風琴鋼琴的發聲體依來源記載使用非常薄的木條，取代前身所用的金屬簧片或彈簧；此材質: According to the source, the sounding element is a very thin slip of wood, replacing the metal reeds or springs used in its predecessor; that change of material makes the timbre softer and sweeter. The instrument also has a keyboard, a pedal and a set of bellows, but the source does not state the materials of the body, keyboard, pedal, bellows or other parts, so all that can be confirmed is that the sounding element is of thin wood; the other materials are not recorded.
風琴鋼琴音色較柔、較甜，發聲簧片或彈簧改用極薄木材而非金屬；鍵盤與踏板驅動每音一: The Aeolsklavier's timbre is softer and sweeter because the sounding reed or spring is of extremely thin wood instead of metal; the keyboard and pedal drive a separate bellows for each note, producing a soft, airy sound. The aeolodion has a range of six octaves and a timbre close to the reed organ; how volume is controlled is not recorded, only that the pedal drives the bellows. Compared with others of the family, the aeolomelodicon added brass pipes to the reeds, like the reed stops of a pipe organ, and was loud; the aeolopantalon was combined with a piano and could be used alone or together with it.
